weeks.headline: Your pregnancy has begun. Your baby is tiny, but a lot is already happening.
weeks.baby: The first parts of my brain, spinal cord and nerves are starting to form. My cells are multiplying fast, and every day I grow a little more.
weeks.body: Your body is already making lots of pregnancy hormones, even though nothing shows on the outside yet.
weeks.feel: Joy, disbelief and worry often come all at once. It's big news, and it takes time to sink in.
weeks.selfCare: Rest, drink plenty of water and take your prenatal vitamins every day.
weeks.reassurance: Lots of women don't feel very pregnant yet. That's completely normal.
weeks.whyNow: The neural tube, which becomes your baby's brain and spinal cord, is forming now.

superfood.benefit: Full of folate, iron and protein, which help your baby's early growth.
superfood.how: Soak it overnight and have it as a morning snack or chaat.

weeks.meal: Palak dal with roti, and a few orange slices.
weeks.doThis: Start your prenatal vitamins, book your first doctor's visit and begin noting how you feel.
weeks.skip: Missing your folic acid, or spending hours online comparing your pregnancy with others.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you have heavy bleeding, severe pain in your tummy, fainting, or pain on one side of your pelvis.

myth.myth: You need to eat for two straight away.
myth.truth: You don't need to eat for two in early pregnancy. What you eat matters far more than how much.

weeks.partner: Celebrate the news with her, and tell her you're in this together.

weeks.headline: Your baby is about the size of a sesame seed. This week the heart, brain and spine are beginning to form.
weeks.baby: I'm growing fast. The tube that will become my brain and spine is forming, and a tiny tube that will become my heart is starting to take shape. Soon it will begin to beat. The early buds of my face and body are just beginning.
weeks.body: Your period is late, and pregnancy hormones are rising quickly. Nothing shows on the outside yet, but you may feel tired, have sore breasts or need to wee more often.
weeks.feel: You may feel happy, shocked, worried, or all three in one afternoon. That's normal when news this big is still sinking in.
weeks.selfCare: Take a folic acid tablet every day, rest when you're tired, and sip water through the day. Small, frequent meals help if you feel queasy.
weeks.reassurance: Many women feel almost nothing at five weeks, and others feel a lot. Both are normal. How you feel isn't a measure of how your pregnancy is going.
weeks.whyNow: Your baby's brain and spine are forming right now, and folate (folic acid) helps them form well. Keep taking your folic acid tablet and add folate-rich food.

superfood.benefit: A good source of folate and iron, both needed in these early weeks.
superfood.how: Try palak dal, palak paratha or a little palak in your khichdi. Wash it well and cook it through.

weeks.meal: Moong dal khichdi with a spoon of ghee, a small bowl of curd and a few pieces of orange. Easy on a queasy stomach.
weeks.doThis: Book your first visit with a doctor, keep taking folic acid every day, and tell your doctor about any medicines you take.
weeks.skip: Alcohol, smoking and any medicine your doctor hasn't said is safe, including herbal ones.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor or go to hospital straight away if you have heavy bleeding, strong pain on one side of your tummy, pain in the tip of your shoulder, or you feel faint.

myth.myth: If you don't feel sick, something must be wrong.
myth.truth: Not feeling sick doesn't mean something is wrong. Many healthy pregnancies come with little or no nausea, and how sick you feel says nothing about how your baby is doing.

weeks.partner: Help her book the first doctor's visit, remind her about folic acid, and take on more of the cooking and housework if she's tired or queasy.

weeks.headline: Your baby's heart is beating in a steady rhythm, and the main organs are starting to take shape.
weeks.baby: My heart beats in a regular rhythm and my brain is growing fast. The first parts of my eyes, ears, arms and legs are starting to form. I'm tiny, but lots of important parts of me are already being built.
weeks.body: Your pregnancy hormones are rising fast, and your body is working hard in the background for your baby.
weeks.feel: You may feel excited one minute and worn out the next. Ups and downs are common this week.
weeks.selfCare: Take it one day at a time. Resting is real work in pregnancy.
weeks.reassurance: How strong your symptoms are doesn't tell you how healthy your pregnancy is.
weeks.whyNow: Nausea often peaks around now, while your baby's organs keep forming fast.

superfood.benefit: Gives you protein, iron and steady energy when you don't feel like eating.
superfood.how: Mix it with water, lemon and roasted jeera for a cool drink.

weeks.meal: A banana oats bowl with a glass of sattu drink.
weeks.doThis: Keep dry snacks close by, eat small meals often, and keep sipping water.
weeks.skip: Forcing down big meals, or ignoring signs that you're dehydrated.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you can't keep fluids down for more than 24 hours, or if you have severe vomiting, heavy bleeding, severe pain in your tummy or fainting.

myth.myth: Feeling very sick means a healthier baby.
myth.truth: Feeling very sick doesn't mean your baby is any healthier. Nausea depends on your hormones, and it differs a lot from woman to woman.

weeks.partner: Take over small daily jobs, and make sure she always has water and snacks close by.

weeks.headline: Your baby's face is starting to take shape, and tiny arms and legs keep growing.
weeks.baby: My brain is growing fast. Tiny buds that will become my arms and legs are growing, and my eyes, ears and nose are taking clearer shape. My heart keeps beating strongly.
weeks.body: Your uterus is growing, even if nothing shows yet. Hormones are still changing your energy, digestion and appetite.
weeks.feel: You may feel excited one minute and worried the next. Ups and downs are a normal part of early pregnancy.
weeks.selfCare: Keep drinking water, and don't feel guilty about needing more rest.
weeks.reassurance: Every pregnancy is different. Some women have lots of symptoms, and others have very few.
weeks.whyNow: Vomiting and nausea can make you lose fluid, so drinking enough matters more now.

superfood.benefit: Keeps you hydrated, gives you natural salts (electrolytes), and is easy on your stomach.
superfood.how: One fresh glass mid-morning.

weeks.meal: Cucumber salad with coconut water and fresh fruit.
weeks.doThis: Keep drinking water, keep taking your prenatal supplements, and take short walks if you feel up to it.
weeks.skip: Comparing your symptoms or your pregnancy with anyone else's.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you have heavy bleeding, severe pain in your tummy, vomiting that won't stop, fever, or signs of dehydration.

myth.myth: Every pregnant woman should feel the same symptoms.
myth.truth: Healthy pregnancies can come with very different symptoms. So if yours don't match a friend's or your sister's, that's okay.

weeks.partner: Listen properly, without rushing to fix every worry.

weeks.headline: All of your baby's main organs have started to form. In about two weeks, your baby will be called a fetus.
weeks.baby: My fingers and toes are starting to form, my face is easier to recognise, and all my main organs have begun growing. The groundwork is ready for my next stage.
weeks.body: Your uterus is now about the size of an orange. Hormones are still changing your digestion, energy and appetite.
weeks.feel: Many women feel excited and unsure at the same time as the first big scan comes closer.
weeks.selfCare: Aim to feed yourself well, not perfectly. Small healthy choices add up.
weeks.reassurance: The first trimester can feel long and hard, but your baby is growing a lot every day.
weeks.whyNow: Your baby's main organs are forming, and they need a steady supply of nutrients.

superfood.benefit: Gives you protein and folate, and it's easy to digest in early pregnancy.
superfood.how: As moong dal khichdi or moong dal soup.

weeks.meal: Moong dal khichdi with curd and vegetables.
weeks.doThis: Write down questions for your next visit, keep eating well, and rest when you can.
weeks.skip: Deciding that every symptom, or no symptom, means something is wrong.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you have heavy bleeding, severe pain in your tummy, vomiting that leaves you dehydrated, fever, or severe dizziness.

myth.myth: Morning sickness only happens in the morning.
myth.truth: Morning sickness can come at any time of day, not only in the morning. Small meals, eaten often, help many women whatever the hour.

weeks.partner: Go to appointments with her when you can, and tell her it's normal to feel anxious.

weeks.headline: Your baby is starting to move, stretch and wiggle, though you can't feel it yet.
weeks.baby: My arms and legs are getting longer, my joints are forming, and I'm starting to make small movements. My heart now has four chambers and works hard every day.
weeks.body: Your body is making more blood for your baby. Hormones are still changing your energy and digestion.
weeks.feel: You may feel more connected to your pregnancy, while still wondering what's ahead.
weeks.selfCare: Listen to your body. Rest when you need to, and don't feel guilty about slowing down.
weeks.reassurance: Many women worry because they can't feel the baby yet. Right now, the movements are still too small to notice.
weeks.whyNow: Your baby's brain is growing fast and needs a steady supply of nutrients.

superfood.benefit: Give you protein, healthy fats and choline, which help early brain growth.
superfood.how: Roasted as a snack, or mixed into chaat.

weeks.meal: Soybean pulao with curd and salad.
weeks.doThis: Keep taking your prenatal vitamins, drink enough water, and go to bed around the same time each night.
weeks.skip: Panicking if your symptoms change from day to day.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you have heavy bleeding, severe pain in your tummy, fainting, fever, or vomiting that leaves you dehydrated.

myth.myth: If your symptoms ease, something is wrong.
myth.truth: Symptoms often ease towards the end of the first 3 months, and that is normal. If you have pain or bleeding, call your doctor.

weeks.partner: Comfort her, rather than trying to solve every worry.

weeks.headline: Your baby's fingers, toes and tiny face are getting clearer every day.
weeks.baby: My fingers and toes are separating, my jaw and face are forming, and my brain keeps making millions of new connections. I can even make tiny movements, though you can't feel them yet.
weeks.body: You're making more blood each week, and your body is working hard for your baby's fast growth. Some women notice their clothes fit a little differently.
weeks.feel: You may feel more connected to your pregnancy, and still unsure about what's ahead.
weeks.selfCare: Build small healthy habits. You don't have to do everything perfectly.
weeks.reassurance: Every pregnancy looks different. Comparing yours with someone else's rarely tells you anything useful.
weeks.whyNow: Your baby is building tissue, muscle and organs fast, and that needs steady protein and iron.

superfood.benefit: Gives you good protein and calcium for your baby's fast growth.
superfood.how: Paneer bhurji, paneer tikka, or added to your sabzi.

weeks.meal: Paneer bhurji with roti and cucumber salad.
weeks.doThis: Put your medical reports in order, keep up your healthy routines, and keep taking your prenatal vitamins.
weeks.skip: Stopping your supplements because you feel better.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you have heavy bleeding, severe pain in your tummy, vomiting that leaves you dehydrated, fever, or fainting.

myth.myth: Exercise in pregnancy is dangerous.
myth.truth: Most healthy pregnancies do well with exercise that your doctor has said is fine. You can ask at your next check-up what suits you.

weeks.partner: Help keep track of appointments, reports and what's coming up next.

weeks.headline: Your baby is more active now, and many body systems are starting to work together.
weeks.baby: My fingers and toes are fully separate, my bones are starting to harden, and I can stretch, kick and move about in my tiny world. My face looks more like me every day.
weeks.body: Your uterus keeps growing, and your body is making more blood to feed your baby.
weeks.feel: You may feel more sure of yourself than a few weeks ago. Worrying now and then is still completely normal.
weeks.selfCare: Sleep, water and gentle movement. These small habits set you up well for the months ahead.
weeks.reassurance: Every woman feels pregnancy differently. There's no right way to feel.
weeks.whyNow: Pregnancy hormones can slow your digestion and make constipation more likely.

superfood.benefit: Full of fibre and vitamin C, so it helps your digestion and your immunity.
superfood.how: Fresh slices as a snack, or in a fruit chaat.

weeks.meal: Vegetable oats upma with some guava on the side.
weeks.doThis: Get enough sleep, keep up your healthy routines, and notice how far you've already come.
weeks.skip: Comparing your bump, symptoms or weight gain with anyone else's.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you have heavy bleeding, severe pain in your tummy, vomiting that won't stop, fever, fainting, or severe dehydration.

myth.myth: Every pregnancy bump should look the same.
myth.truth: Bumps come in all shapes and sizes, and they differ from woman to woman and pregnancy to pregnancy. There's no right way for yours to look.

weeks.partner: Notice how far she's come, not only what's next.

weeks.headline: You've reached a big milestone. Your baby's organs have formed, and the first trimester is nearly over.
weeks.baby: Most of my main organs have formed and are starting to work. I can move my arms and legs, open and close my tiny fingers, and my reflexes grow every day.
weeks.body: Your uterus is much bigger now, and your body has changed a lot to care for your baby.
weeks.feel: Many women feel relief, gratitude and new confidence as the first trimester ends.
weeks.selfCare: Take a moment to notice everything your body has done in the last three months.
weeks.reassurance: The first trimester can feel long and tiring. Reaching this point is worth celebrating.
weeks.whyNow: Your blood volume is rising fast to feed your baby and the placenta.

superfood.benefit: Full of vitamin C, which helps your body take in iron and supports your immunity.
superfood.how: Fresh, as juice, or in a chutney.

weeks.meal: Rajma rice with salad and a fresh amla.
weeks.doThis: Celebrate finishing the first trimester, check your upcoming appointments, and keep up your healthy habits.
weeks.skip: Dropping your healthy routines just because some symptoms are easing.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you have heavy bleeding, severe pain in your tummy, vomiting that leaves you dehydrated, fever, a severe headache or fainting.

myth.myth: After the first 3 months, the hard part is over.
myth.truth: Many women feel better in months 4 to 6, but your body is still working hard. Keep resting when you need to, and keep going to your check-ups.

weeks.partner: Tell her you see everything she's been through, and celebrate this milestone with her.

weeks.headline: Welcome to the second trimester. Your baby is growing fast, and many women start to feel more energy.
weeks.baby: My vocal cords are forming, my fingerprints are starting to appear, and my bones keep getting stronger. I can move around freely in my tiny world.
weeks.body: For many women, nausea starts to ease and energy slowly comes back. Your uterus keeps growing up and out of your pelvis.
weeks.feel: Relief and excitement often take the place of some of the first trimester's worry.
weeks.selfCare: Use your returning energy to set up habits that will carry you through the second trimester.
weeks.reassurance: Every pregnancy moves at its own pace. It's normal if your symptoms haven't changed much yet.
weeks.whyNow: Your baby is growing faster, and your body is making more blood than ever.

superfood.benefit: Gives you iron, folate and antioxidants that help healthy growth.
superfood.how: Palak dal, palak paneer, or blended into soup.

weeks.meal: Palak paneer with roti and cucumber salad.
weeks.doThis: Take your first bump photo, start a pregnancy journal, and celebrate reaching the second trimester.
weeks.skip: Feeling guilty when pregnancy doesn't feel exciting every day.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you have heavy bleeding, severe pain in your tummy, fever, severe headaches, or sudden swelling.

myth.myth: Good mothers feel bonded to their baby straight away.
myth.truth: Bonding grows differently for everyone, and often slowly, over time. If the feeling doesn't come straight away, it doesn't make you any less of a good mother.

weeks.partner: Suggest things she enjoys and may have missed in the first trimester.

weeks.headline: Your baby's face can make tiny expressions now, and small movements happen all day.
weeks.baby: The muscles in my face are growing, so I can make tiny expressions. My neck is getting stronger, and for the first time my body is growing faster than my head.
weeks.body: Your uterus is growing steadily, and your bump may start to show. Many women have more energy now.
weeks.feel: You may feel closer to your baby as other people start to see you're pregnant.
weeks.selfCare: Mind your posture. Your centre of balance is slowly starting to shift.
weeks.reassurance: Not showing yet is completely normal. Every body shows pregnancy differently.
weeks.whyNow: Your baby's bones are getting stronger, and they need steady calcium and protein.

superfood.benefit: One of India's richest natural sources of calcium, with fibre and iron too.
superfood.how: Ragi dosa, ragi porridge or ragi roti.

weeks.meal: Ragi dosa with curd and vegetable chutney.
weeks.doThis: Take a bump photo each week, keep up gentle exercise, and stick with your healthy routines.
weeks.skip: Buying every baby product you see online.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you have heavy bleeding, severe pain in your tummy, headaches that won't go, fever, or fluid leaking.

myth.myth: A bigger bump means a bigger baby.
myth.truth: A bigger bump doesn't reliably tell you your baby's size. Bump size depends on lots of things, and your scans show how your baby is growing.

weeks.partner: Notice her changing body, and be kind and encouraging about it.

weeks.headline: Your baby's body is growing quickly, and tiny movements are getting smoother every day.
weeks.baby: My muscles and bones are getting stronger. I can move my arms, legs and joints more smoothly now. My ears are forming, and I'm getting ready to hear the world around me in the coming weeks.
weeks.body: Your bump may show more now. Extra blood flow can give your skin a healthy glow, and your growing uterus may cause the odd stretching feeling.
weeks.feel: Many women feel more settled and hopeful around now, and start picturing life after the birth.
weeks.selfCare: Keep moving gently, and watch your posture as your body changes.
weeks.reassurance: Mild stretching and pulling feelings are common as your uterus grows to make room for your baby.
weeks.whyNow: Your baby's bones and future teeth are forming fast, and they need calcium and vitamin D.

superfood.benefit: Gives you calcium, healthy fats and minerals that help bones grow.
superfood.how: Til laddoo, sprinkled over salad, or mixed into chutney.

weeks.meal: Ragi porridge with nuts and a bowl of curd.
weeks.doThis: Talk to your baby every day, keep up your healthy routines, and make time to relax.
weeks.skip: Brushing off stress, or trying to keep up your pre-pregnancy pace.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you have bleeding, severe pain in your tummy, fluid leaking, severe headaches that won't go, or fever.

myth.myth: Your baby can't hear you yet, so talking doesn't matter.
myth.truth: Your baby's ears are forming now, and soon they'll hear your voice. So it's a lovely time to start talking to your baby.

weeks.partner: Join her in talking, reading or singing to the baby.

weeks.headline: Your baby is getting stronger, and the tiny parts needed for hearing are growing.
weeks.baby: My bones are hardening, my muscles are getting stronger, and my ears are growing fast. Soon I'll start reacting to sounds from outside.
weeks.body: Your uterus keeps growing, and your bump may be easy to see now. Some women notice more energy and a healthy glow.
weeks.feel: Many women feel more confident and settled around now.
weeks.selfCare: Watch your posture and wear supportive shoes as your centre of balance shifts.
weeks.reassurance: Mild aches and stretching feelings are often just your body adjusting to pregnancy.
weeks.whyNow: Your baby's skeleton is getting stronger fast, as soft cartilage turns into bone.

superfood.benefit: Gives you calcium, iron and fibre to help bones grow well.
superfood.how: Ragi dosa, ragi porridge or ragi roti.

weeks.meal: Ragi cheela with curd and mint chutney.
weeks.doThis: Spend time outdoors, keep moving every day, and start talking to your baby often.
weeks.skip: Standing for a long time without a break.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you have bleeding, severe pain in your tummy, fluid leaking, severe headaches, or sudden swelling.

myth.myth: If you feel good, you don't need extra rest.
myth.truth: Your body is still doing a lot of work, even when your symptoms ease. So rest when you can, even on the days you feel good.

weeks.partner: Back her healthy routines, and encourage her to rest when she needs it.

weeks.headline: Your baby's skeleton is getting stronger, a little body fat is forming, and movements are getting smoother.
weeks.baby: My skeleton is changing from soft cartilage into stronger bone. My muscles are getting stronger, and I'm practising the movements that help me grow.
weeks.body: Your bump is showing more, and your uterus keeps growing upward. You're making a lot more blood now for your baby.
weeks.feel: Excitement often grows around now, as women start waiting for the first movements they can feel.
weeks.selfCare: Stand up slowly, and keep drinking water through the day.
weeks.reassurance: Not feeling movement yet is completely normal. Many first-time mothers won't feel kicks for a few more weeks.
weeks.whyNow: Your baby's muscles are growing fast, and they need steady protein and minerals.

superfood.benefit: Gives you good plant protein and minerals that help muscles grow.
superfood.how: Moong dal khichdi, dal soup or moong chilla.

weeks.meal: Moong dal chilla stuffed with paneer and vegetables.
weeks.doThis: Notice any new feelings in your tummy, and keep building your healthy daily routines.
weeks.skip: Worrying if you haven't felt the baby move yet.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you have heavy bleeding, severe pain in your tummy, fluid leaking, severe headaches, fever, or a lot of swelling.

myth.myth: Every mother feels her baby move by Week 17.
myth.truth: When you first feel your baby move varies a lot, especially in a first pregnancy. If you haven't felt anything yet, your doctor can talk you through what to expect.

weeks.partner: Share her excitement, and remind her that every pregnancy keeps its own timing.

weeks.headline: Your baby's ears are growing, and the brain is building the links that help with learning and memory.
weeks.baby: My ears are growing fast, and my brain is making millions of new connections. I can move my arms and legs with more control, and my nerves are getting more skilled.
weeks.body: Your uterus keeps growing, and your centre of balance is slowly shifting. Many women notice changes in their posture and balance.
weeks.feel: Excitement often builds as the anomaly scan comes closer, and the baby feels more real than ever.
weeks.selfCare: Watch your posture, and try not to stand in one spot for too long.
weeks.reassurance: Feeling excited and nervous before the anomaly scan is completely normal.
weeks.whyNow: Your baby's brain and nerves are growing fast, and healthy fats help.

superfood.benefit: One of the best vegetarian sources of omega-3 fats, which help the brain grow.
superfood.how: Add ground flaxseed to your atta, curd or smoothies.

weeks.meal: A curd bowl with flaxseed powder, walnuts and seasonal fruit.
weeks.doThis: Write down your questions for the anomaly scan, and keep talking or reading to your baby.
weeks.skip: Spending hours online reading worst-case pregnancy stories.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you have heavy bleeding, severe pain in your tummy, fluid leaking, fever, severe headaches, or sudden swelling.

myth.myth: The anomaly scan is mainly about finding out the baby's sex.
myth.truth: The anomaly scan is done to check how your baby is growing and developing. In India, it's against the law to tell parents the baby's sex.

weeks.partner: Help her write down questions, and comfort her if she feels anxious.

weeks.headline: Your baby's senses are sharpening, and a protective coating for their skin is starting to form.
weeks.baby: My brain keeps growing fast and my senses are getting sharper. A protective coating called vernix is starting to form on my skin. My arms and legs are stronger, and I'm more active.
weeks.body: Your uterus is now nearly level with your belly button. Many women feel more stretching as the baby and uterus keep growing.
weeks.feel: You may feel excited about the anomaly scan, and wonder what the second half of pregnancy will bring.
weeks.selfCare: Take short breaks through the day to stretch and change position, especially if you sit for long.
weeks.reassurance: Your baby gets stronger and more developed every day. A lot of growing happens in these weeks.
weeks.whyNow: Healthy fats and foods rich in antioxidants help your baby's skin, nerves and overall growth.

superfood.benefit: Give you vitamin E, healthy fats and antioxidants that help skin and nerves grow.
superfood.how: Have 5 to 6 soaked almonds a day.

weeks.meal: A bowl of curd topped with chopped almonds, walnuts and seasonal fruit.
weeks.doThis: Get ready for your anomaly scan in your own way, and keep building your bond with your baby.
weeks.skip: Reading frightening stories online before or after your scan.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you have heavy bleeding, severe pain in your tummy, fluid leaking, fever, severe headaches, or sudden swelling.

myth.myth: Every scan finds problems.
myth.truth: Most scans are routine, and they usually show that your baby is growing as expected. It's normal to feel a little nervous before one all the same.

weeks.partner: Stay calm and supportive, and give her space to talk about her thoughts and worries.

weeks.headline: You're halfway through your pregnancy. For many women, this is the week of the anatomy scan.
weeks.baby: I can hear sounds now, swallow amniotic fluid, and move my arms and legs on purpose. At the anomaly scan, the doctors will check carefully how I'm growing.
weeks.body: Your uterus is now close to your belly button. Many women feel stronger kicks, stretching, and the odd ache along the sides of the bump (round ligament pain).
weeks.feel: Excitement and nerves often come together this week. The anomaly scan feels big because it gives a detailed look at how your baby is growing.
weeks.selfCare: If your anomaly scan is this week, keep the rest of that day light. Give yourself time to take it in, and mark the milestone.
weeks.reassurance: Feeling anxious before the anomaly scan is completely normal. Most scans are routine and show that the baby is growing well.
weeks.whyNow: Your baby is building muscle, organs and tissue fast, and growth speeds up in the second half of pregnancy.

superfood.benefit: Gives you protein and iron for the fast growth of the second half of pregnancy.
superfood.how: Kala chana curry, boiled chana chaat, or sprouts.

weeks.meal: Palak paneer with roti and a bowl of curd.
weeks.doThis: Mark your halfway point, go to your anomaly scan, and keep a memory of the day.
weeks.skip: Spending hours online reading worst-case stories before or after your scan.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you have heavy bleeding, severe pain in your tummy, fluid that keeps leaking, a severe headache with changes in your vision, or if your baby suddenly moves much less after a regular pattern has already set in.

myth.myth: If the anomaly scan shows something, it's always serious.
myth.truth: A finding on the anomaly scan isn't always serious. Many findings are small, and some settle on their own. Your doctor will explain what it means and whether you need another scan.

weeks.partner: Go to the anomaly scan with her if you can. Listen more than you talk, and help her mark the milestone.

weeks.headline: Your baby is noticing more of the world inside the womb, and starting to sense taste and touch.
weeks.baby: My taste buds are forming, I swallow more amniotic fluid, and my movements are stronger and smoother. My brain keeps making millions of new connections.
weeks.body: Your bump is showing more, and movements may feel stronger and more regular. Your body keeps adjusting to your baby's fast growth.
weeks.feel: Many women feel closer to their baby as the movements come more often and are easier to feel.
weeks.selfCare: Pause during the day to notice your baby moving, and enjoy those moments together.
weeks.reassurance: Your baby's movement pattern is still forming. Some days feel busier than others.
weeks.whyNow: Your baby's brain keeps growing fast, and a steady supply of healthy fats helps.

superfood.benefit: Give you omega-3 fats, which help the brain grow.
superfood.how: 2 to 4 walnut halves a day as a snack.

weeks.meal: A curd bowl topped with walnuts, flaxseed powder and seasonal fruit.
weeks.doThis: Spend a few minutes each day talking, singing or reading to your baby.
weeks.skip: Ignoring leg cramps that keep coming back, or not drinking enough.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you have heavy bleeding, fluid leaking, severe pain in your tummy, severe headaches, or sudden swelling.

myth.myth: Babies in the womb don't notice anything around them.
myth.truth: Your baby is already learning to hear, move, taste and react to the world around them. Your voice is part of that world now.

weeks.partner: Stop what you're doing and share the moments when the baby is active.

weeks.headline: Your baby can now hear sounds from inside and outside the womb, including your voice.
weeks.baby: My hearing is growing fast, and I can now pick up sounds like your heartbeat, your voice and even some noises from outside. My brain keeps learning from all of it.
weeks.body: Your baby is growing steadily, and you may feel movements more often through the day. Your centre of balance keeps shifting as your bump grows.
weeks.feel: Many women feel a stronger bond once they know their baby can hear their voice.
weeks.selfCare: Spend a few calm minutes each day talking, reading or singing to your baby.
weeks.reassurance: There's no perfect way to bond with your baby. Small moments every day matter most.
weeks.whyNow: Your baby's brain keeps growing fast, and needs nutrients that help memory, learning and the nerves.

superfood.benefit: Give you protein and choline, which help the brain grow.
superfood.how: Soya chunks curry, soybean pulao, or roasted soya snacks.

weeks.meal: Soybean pulao with curd and vegetable salad.
weeks.doThis: Start a small daily habit with your baby, like reading a short story, singing or talking.
weeks.skip: Thinking bonding only starts after birth.
weeks.redFlags: Call your doctor if you have heavy bleeding, fluid leaking, severe pain in your tummy, severe headaches, changes in your vision, or sudden swelling.

myth.myth: Babies can't hear clearly until late pregnancy.
myth.truth: By now, your baby can already hear sounds and react to them. So this is a nice time to talk, sing or read to your baby.

weeks.partner: Talk to the baby often, and make time for these moments together.

weeks.headline: Your baby's brain is making millions of new connections, and learning has already begun.

1.q: What happens in the first month of pregnancy?
a: In the first month, roughly weeks 1 to 4 counted from your last period, a great deal is happening even before a bump or many symptoms appear. The fertilised egg travels to the womb and settles in, and often the first thing you notice is a missed period.
takeaways: Month 1 is weeks 1 to 4, counted from your last period.
The egg implants in the womb and hCG begins to rise.
Many women feel nothing beyond a missed period.
Confirm with a test and start folic acid.
Book your first doctor visit.

1.q: How is my baby developing in the first month?
a: In the first month your baby grows from a single fertilised cell into a tiny embryo about the size of a poppy seed, roughly 2 mm, by the end of week 4.
takeaways: Grows from one cell to a roughly 2 mm embryo.
Three cell layers form the future organs.
The neural tube (brain and spine) begins to form.
Too early to see anything on a scan.
Folic acid protects this exact stage.

1.q: When is a home pregnancy test accurate, and what is the beta hCG blood test?
a: A home pregnancy test is usually accurate from the first day of your missed period, and most reliable with your first morning urine. A beta hCG blood test can confirm pregnancy a little earlier and can also measure the exact hormone level.
takeaways: Home tests are accurate from the missed period, using first morning urine.
hCG doubles every two to three days.
A blood beta hCG test detects earlier and measures the level.
Testing too early can give a false negative.
Retest in a few days if negative but your period is late.

1.q: Do I need a scan this early, and when is the first one?
a: You usually do not need a scan in the very first month. The first ultrasound, often called the dating or viability scan, is typically done around 6 to 8 weeks, once there is something to see.
takeaways: Usually no scan is needed in Month 1.
The first dating or viability scan is around 6 to 8 weeks.
The heartbeat cannot be seen much before then.
Early scans are often done transvaginally.
Book your first doctor visit first.

1.q: Should I start folic acid now, and how much?
a: Yes, start folic acid as soon as you know you are pregnant, and ideally even before, if you are planning. The usual dose is 400 to 500 micrograms a day, continued through at least the first trimester.
takeaways: Start as soon as you know, ideally before conception.
Usual dose is 400 to 500 mcg daily.
ICMR recommends around 500 mcg.
It protects the baby's developing brain and spine.
Some women need a higher dose, so check with your doctor.

1.q: What should I eat, and what should I avoid, in early pregnancy?
a: In early pregnancy, focus on a balanced everyday diet rich in folate, iron, calcium and protein, and be careful mainly with a short list of foods that carry an infection or contamination risk.
takeaways: Eat folate, iron, calcium and protein rich foods.
Avoid raw or undercooked meat, eggs and seafood.
Choose pasteurised dairy and low-mercury fish.
Wash produce, cook well, and be careful with street food.
Skip green, unripe papaya.

1.q: Can I drink tea, coffee or alcohol in early pregnancy?
a: You can still enjoy tea and coffee in moderation, keeping total caffeine under about 200 mg a day, roughly one cup of coffee or two small cups of tea. Alcohol, though, is best avoided completely in pregnancy.
takeaways: Keep caffeine under about 200 mg a day, roughly one coffee.
Tea and chai in moderation are fine.
Watch hidden caffeine in cola, chocolate and energy drinks.
Avoid alcohol entirely.
Do not panic about drinks you had before knowing.

1.q: What early pregnancy symptoms are normal in the first month?
a: In the first month, many women feel nothing beyond a missed period, while others notice tender breasts, tiredness, mild nausea, bloating or a little cramping. All of this is normal.
takeaways: A missed period is often the first sign.
Tender breasts, fatigue, mild nausea and bloating are common.
Nausea usually starts around weeks 5 to 6.
Feeling little is also completely normal.
Rest, hydrate and eat small, regular meals.

1.q: Is light spotting or bleeding normal in early pregnancy?
a: Light spotting in early pregnancy is common and often harmless, and it can happen as the embryo implants. It is still always worth mentioning any bleeding to your doctor so they can check.
takeaways: Light spotting is common and often harmless.
It can happen as the embryo implants.
Up to one in four women bleed in the first trimester.
Any bleeding is worth mentioning to your doctor.
Heavier bleeding or strong pain needs prompt review.

1.q: Can I exercise and travel in early pregnancy?
a: Yes, in an uncomplicated pregnancy you can usually keep exercising and travelling in early pregnancy. Gentle, regular activity is actually encouraged, and most travel is fine as long as you feel well.
takeaways: Gentle, regular exercise is encouraged.
Aim for about 150 minutes a week of moderate activity.
Favour walking, swimming and prenatal yoga.
Avoid overheating and stay hydrated.
Most early travel is fine; move your legs on long trips.

1.q: How is pregnancy counted, and how many weeks am I?
a: Pregnancy is counted in weeks from the first day of your last period, not from the day you conceived. That is why you are already about four weeks pregnant by the time you miss a period, and why an app may show a higher week than you expected.
takeaways: Counted from the first day of your last period.
You are about 4 weeks along at your missed period.
The pregnancy week runs about 2 weeks ahead of conception.
Around 40 weeks total, roughly nine months.
A scan confirms your dates if periods are irregular.

1.q: What are the signs of an ectopic pregnancy?
a: An ectopic pregnancy is when the fertilised egg settles outside the womb, most often in a fallopian tube. It is uncommon, but because it cannot grow safely there, it needs to be found and looked after. The signs worth knowing are one-sided lower tummy pain, unusual bleeding, and pain at the tip of the shoulder.
takeaways: The pregnancy is outside the womb, usually in a tube.
The pregnancy test is still positive.
Signs are one-sided pain, unusual bleeding, shoulder-tip pain.
It usually shows between 4 and 12 weeks.
An early scan and blood test confirm where the pregnancy is.

1.q: Can I have pregnancy symptoms before a missed period?
a: Some women do notice early signs, like tender breasts, tiredness, mild cramps or a heightened sense of smell, in the days before a missed period. But many feel nothing yet, and a missed period remains the most reliable early clue.
takeaways: Some early signs can appear before a missed period.
Tender breasts, fatigue, mild cramps, smell sensitivity.
They overlap heavily with normal pre-period symptoms.
Symptoms cannot confirm pregnancy; only a test can.
Test from your missed period, using morning urine.

1.q: Is white discharge in early pregnancy normal?
a: A mild increase in thin, milky-white discharge is normal and common in early pregnancy. It is called leukorrhea, and it is actually a good sign, part of how your body protects against infection.
takeaways: Thin, milky-white discharge is normal in early pregnancy.
It is called leukorrhea and helps prevent infection.
Normal discharge has no itching, burning or strong smell.
Use cotton liners; avoid douching and scented products.
See your doctor for green, yellow, cottage-cheese, foul-smelling or itchy discharge.

1.q: Can sex or orgasm cause a miscarriage in early pregnancy?
a: In a normal, uncomplicated pregnancy, sex and orgasm do not cause miscarriage. Your baby is well protected inside the womb, so intimacy is generally safe unless your doctor has advised otherwise.
takeaways: Sex and orgasm do not cause miscarriage in a normal pregnancy.
The baby is protected by the womb, sac and mucus plug.
Mild cramps or light spotting after sex can be normal.
Use a condom if there is any infection risk.
Check with your doctor if you have bleeding or specific conditions.

1.q: What happens at my first doctor (antenatal) visit?
a: Your first antenatal visit, ideally around 6 to 8 weeks, is the longest and most thorough of your pregnancy. Your doctor takes your history, does a basic check-up, arranges your first blood tests, and starts you on folic acid.
takeaways: Ideally at 6 to 8 weeks; the longest visit.
Covers history, a check-up, your dates and folic acid.
Booking blood tests are arranged.
Bring records, a medicines list, your LMP date and questions.
Mention IVF or IUI if relevant.

1.q: What blood tests are done in early pregnancy?
a: Early in pregnancy your doctor orders a set of routine booking blood tests. These usually include a blood count, your blood group and Rh, thyroid, blood sugar, and screening for infections like HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis, along with a urine test.
takeaways: Routine bloods include blood count, blood group and Rh, thyroid, blood sugar.
Infection screening covers HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis.
A urine test is done too.
Most happen at your first visit.
Many are available free at government centres.

1.q: How soon can morning sickness start, and what helps?
a: Morning sickness, meaning pregnancy nausea, most often starts around weeks 5 to 6 and usually eases by weeks 12 to 14. Despite the name, it can happen at any time of day, and simple steps often help you through the worst of it.
takeaways: Usually starts around weeks 5 to 6, eases by weeks 12 to 14.
Can happen at any time of day.
Small frequent meals, hydration and ginger often help.
Eat something before getting up.
Ask your doctor if it is severe.

1.q: How is early pregnancy different after IVF?
a: After IVF, early pregnancy is confirmed with a beta hCG blood test about 9 to 14 days after your embryo transfer, and you usually stay under your fertility clinic's care until around 7 to 10 weeks before moving to your regular pregnancy doctor. The pregnancy itself develops much like any other.
takeaways: Beta hCG test about 9 to 14 days after transfer confirms pregnancy.
A rising level matters more than any single number.
A first scan is usually around 6 to 7 weeks.
You move to your OB around 7 to 10 weeks.
The pregnancy develops much like any other, with closer monitoring.

1.q: When is it safe to tell people I'm pregnant?
a: There is no medically fixed rule for when to tell people you are pregnant. Many families in India wait until after the first three months, when the chance of miscarriage has dropped, but the timing is entirely your personal choice.
takeaways: There is no medical rule on when to announce.
Many wait past the first three months as miscarriage risk falls.
Some share early for support, others prefer privacy.
The choice is yours and your partner's.
Family custom need not decide it for you.

1.q: When does my baby's heart start beating?
a: Your baby's heart begins to beat very early, at around 5 to 6 weeks of pregnancy, though it usually cannot be seen on a scan until about 6 to 7 weeks. Early on the rate is slower, then it speeds up over the following weeks.
takeaways: The heart starts beating around 5 to 6 weeks.
It is usually visible on a scan around 6 to 7 weeks.
The early rate is slower, then speeds up.
Not seeing it at a very early scan is often just timing.
A repeat scan is common and reassuring.

1.q: I took a medicine before I knew I was pregnant. Which medicines are safe?
a: If you took a common medicine before you knew you were pregnant, try not to worry, as most everyday medicines cause no harm, especially early on. Going forward, the safest approach is not to take or stop any medicine without checking first with your doctor or pharmacist.
takeaways: Most everyday medicines taken before you knew cause no harm.
Do not start any medicine, including over-the-counter or herbal, without checking first.
Never stop a prescribed medicine on your own.
Keep a note of what you take.
Mention anything you took before you knew at your first visit.

1.q: Why am I so tired in early pregnancy?
a: Feeling very tired in early pregnancy is extremely common and usually harmless. It is largely driven by the rise in the hormone progesterone, and for most women it eases as the first trimester ends.
takeaways: Extreme tiredness is common and usually harmless.
It is driven mainly by rising progesterone.
It often eases in the second trimester.
Rest, gentle activity and good meals help.
Mention it if severe, as anaemia can be a cause.

1.q: Is constipation and bloating normal in early pregnancy?
a: Constipation and bloating are very common in early pregnancy and are usually nothing to worry about. Pregnancy hormones slow the gut down, and iron in prenatal supplements can add to it.
takeaways: Constipation and bloating are common and usually harmless.
Caused by hormones slowing the gut, plus iron supplements.
Fibre, water and gentle movement help.
Ask before using laxatives.
Tell your doctor if it is severe or painful.

1.q: Is mild cramping normal in early pregnancy?
a: Mild cramping in early pregnancy is common and usually normal. It often comes from the womb growing and stretching, and can feel a little like period cramps.
takeaways: Mild cramping is common and usually normal.
It often comes from the womb stretching.
It can feel like gentle period cramps.
Rest, warmth and hydration help.
Get severe, one-sided or bleeding-related cramping checked.

1.q: Why do I have food cravings and aversions?
a: Sudden food cravings and strong dislikes are a very normal part of early pregnancy. They are driven by shifting hormones and a heightened sense of smell, and they usually settle as pregnancy goes on.
takeaways: Cravings and aversions are normal in early pregnancy.
Caused by hormones and a heightened sense of smell.
Follow cravings in moderation; work around aversions.
Use a fan or ask for help if cooking smells trigger you.
Tell your doctor about cravings for non-food items.

1.q: Why do I need to pee so often in early pregnancy?
a: Needing to pee more often is one of the earliest and most common signs of pregnancy, and it is completely normal. It happens because your body makes more blood and your kidneys have more fluid to process.
takeaways: Frequent urination is a normal early sign.
Caused by more blood and busier kidneys.
Later the womb presses on the bladder too.
Keep drinking water, but ease off just before bed.
See your doctor if peeing burns or hurts.

1.q: How do I know if I'm expecting twins?
a: The only reliable way to know you are expecting twins is an ultrasound scan, which can often show two babies from around 6 to 7 weeks. Some women do notice stronger early symptoms, but these alone cannot confirm it.
takeaways: Only a scan reliably confirms twins, often from 6 to 7 weeks.
Stronger symptoms can hint at it but cannot confirm.
Higher chance with IVF, family history, older age or previous twins.
Twins need closer monitoring.
Many twin pregnancies go well.

1.q: How much water should I drink in pregnancy?
a: Aim for roughly 8 to 12 glasses of fluid a day in pregnancy, about 2 to 2.5 litres, a little more than before. All drinks count, and a simple check is that your urine stays a pale, clear colour.
takeaways: Aim for about 8 to 12 glasses (2 to 2.5 litres) a day.
All fluids count.
Pale, clear urine is a good sign.
It helps with constipation, tiredness and headaches.
Sip steadily, especially in the heat or with morning sickness.

1.q: Is it normal to feel anxious or unsure after finding out I'm pregnant?
a: It is completely normal to feel a mix of emotions after finding out you are pregnant, including joy, worry, and even moments of sadness or uncertainty. Wanting a pregnancy and still feeling anxious about it are not contradictions.
takeaways: Mixed feelings in early pregnancy are normal.
You can want a pregnancy and still feel anxious.
Bonding may be immediate or take time.
Reach out if worry or low mood is constant or disruptive.
Sharing with your doctor or someone you trust helps.

1.q: What is Garbh Sanskar?
a: Garbh Sanskar is a traditional Indian practice, rooted in Ayurveda, whose name means "nurturing or educating the baby in the womb." It rests on a sound idea: that what a mother eats, feels and experiences in pregnancy reaches her growing baby and helps shape how the baby develops.
takeaways: Garbh Sanskar means "nurturing the baby in the womb," rooted in Ayurveda.
Much of what you eat, feel and experience reaches your baby.
Nutrition builds the brain, calm lowers stress hormones reaching the baby, and your voice becomes familiar.
It cannot promise a fixed outcome, but supports the best environment for development.
It complements, and never replaces, medical care.

1.q: When should I start Garbh Sanskar, and how do I do it at home?
a: You can start Garbh Sanskar as soon as you know you are pregnant, and some families even begin before conception. There is no single "correct" time, and the first trimester simply focuses on gentle foundations.
takeaways: Start whenever you learn you are pregnant, or earlier.
The first trimester keeps things gentle.
A simple daily rhythm works better than doing everything.
Talking to baby is about bonding; hearing comes later.
Check with your doctor before starting yoga.

1.q: How can I support my baby's brain development during pregnancy?
a: There is a great deal you can do to give your baby's brain the best start, and the early weeks matter most, since this is when the brain first forms. The main levers are good nutrition, a calm and healthy you, and avoiding harmful exposures.
takeaways: The early weeks matter most, as the brain begins forming then.
Building blocks: folate, iron, iodine, choline, omega-3, B12, vitamin D.
Avoiding alcohol and smoking protects development.
Staying calm helps, since your stress reaches the baby.
From mid-pregnancy, your voice, music and reading become real experiences for your baby.

1.q: Are there prayers or duas I can say during pregnancy?
a: Yes, prayers, duas, mantras or any spiritual practice from your faith are welcome during pregnancy, and many families find them deeply comforting. They are a personal choice, and their main benefit is the calm and connection they bring.
takeaways: Prayers, duas and mantras from any faith are welcome.
Their main benefit is calm and connection.
Choose what feels meaningful to you.
Not a replacement for medical care.
Check fasting or strenuous rituals with your doctor.

1.q: What is anemia in pregnancy and how do I prevent it?
a: Anemia means your blood has too little haemoglobin to carry oxygen well, and it is very common in Indian pregnancies, affecting around half of women. The good news is it is usually easy to prevent and treat.
takeaways: Anemia means too little haemoglobin to carry oxygen.
It affects about half of Indian pregnancies.
It is checked by an Hb test at your first visit.
Eat iron-rich foods with vitamin C; avoid tea and coffee at meals.
Take prescribed iron and folic acid, free at government centres.

1.q: Are breast changes normal in early pregnancy?
a: Yes, breast changes are one of the earliest and most common signs of pregnancy. Tenderness, tingling, fullness, and darkening around the nipples are all normal and driven by rising hormones.
takeaways: Breast changes are a common early sign.
Tenderness, tingling, fullness and darker areolas are normal.
Caused by hormones and increased blood flow.
A supportive bra and compresses help.
For any pain relief, check with your doctor first.

1.q: Are headaches normal in early pregnancy?
a: Headaches are common in early pregnancy and are usually harmless. They are linked to hormonal changes, increased blood volume, and sometimes dehydration or missing meals.
takeaways: Headaches are common and usually harmless early on.
Caused by hormones, blood volume, dehydration or skipped meals.
Hydration, regular meals, rest and sleep help.
For any medicine, get your doctor's guidance.
Get severe headaches with vision changes or swelling checked.

1.q: Why do I feel dizzy or lightheaded in early pregnancy?
a: Feeling dizzy or lightheaded is common in early pregnancy and usually harmless. It mostly happens because pregnancy hormones relax your blood vessels and slightly lower your blood pressure.
takeaways: Dizziness is common and usually harmless early on.
Caused by lower blood pressure, low blood sugar, heat or dehydration.
Anemia can contribute.
Rise slowly, eat regularly, hydrate, avoid long standing.
See your doctor if you faint or have bleeding with it.

1.q: Can I fast during pregnancy (Navratri, Karva Chauth, Ramadan)?
a: Whether you can fast during pregnancy depends on your health, and it is best decided with your doctor. For a healthy pregnancy, a short or modified fast is often possible, but it is not advised if you have complications.
takeaways: Fasting can be safe for some healthy pregnancies, with a doctor's okay.
Main risks are dehydration, low blood sugar and nutrient gaps.
Avoid if you have diabetes, high blood pressure, anemia or a high-risk pregnancy.
Prefer a modified fast with fluids and fruits.
Break it if you feel unwell.

1.q: Can I dye my hair or use cosmetics during pregnancy?
a: Colouring your hair is generally considered safe in pregnancy, especially after the first trimester, because your scalp absorbs only a tiny amount of the chemicals. Most everyday cosmetics are fine too, with a few sensible precautions.
takeaways: Hair dye is generally safe, especially after the first trimester.
Scalp absorption is minimal.
Highlights, semi-permanent dye or pure henna lower exposure.
Use gloves, ventilation and a patch test; avoid eyebrows and eyelashes.
Skip strong retinoid creams and check prescription treatments.

1.q: Implantation bleeding vs a period: how do I tell the difference?
a: Implantation bleeding is light pink or brown spotting that some women notice when the embryo settles into the womb, usually around the time a period is due. The easiest way to tell it from a period is that it stays much lighter and shorter and never builds into a full flow.
takeaways: Implantation bleeding is light pink or brown spotting.
It is lighter and shorter than a period, with no clots.
About 1 in 4 women have it, and many do not.
Test from your missed period, not during the spotting.
Get heavy bleeding or pain checked.

1.q: Is brown discharge normal in early pregnancy?
a: Brown discharge in early pregnancy is common and usually harmless. Brown simply means older blood that has taken a little time to leave the body, rather than fresh bleeding.
takeaways: Brown discharge is usually old blood and often harmless.
Common causes: implantation, old blood clearing, a sensitive cervix.
Light and odourless is reassuring.
Watch for heavy red bleeding, pain or a bad smell.
Get those checked with your doctor.

1.q: Are mood swings normal in early pregnancy?
a: Mood swings are very common in early pregnancy and are a normal response to a surge of hormones and a big life change. Feeling weepy, irritable or up and down, sometimes within the same hour, does not mean anything is wrong.
takeaways: Mood swings are normal in early pregnancy.
Driven by hormones plus tiredness and adjustment.
Often strongest around weeks 6 to 10.
Rest, support and honesty with loved ones help.
Reach out if low mood or anxiety is constant or disruptive.

1.q: Why do I have a metallic taste and a heightened sense of smell?
a: A metallic taste in the mouth and a sharper sense of smell are common, if odd, early pregnancy symptoms. Both are driven mainly by rising hormones, and both usually fade by the second trimester.
takeaways: Metallic taste (dysgeusia) and sharper smell are common and harmless.
Driven by rising estrogen and increased blood flow.
Often start early and ease by the second trimester.
Citrus, mints, cold foods and oral care help.
Mention a supplement that seems to worsen it.

1.q: Can I sleep on my back or stomach in early pregnancy?
a: In early pregnancy you can sleep in whatever position is comfortable, including on your back or stomach. Your baby is still small and well protected, so there is no need to worry about your sleep position yet.
takeaways: Any position is fine in early pregnancy, including back and stomach.
The baby is still small and protected.
Side sleeping matters more from around mid-pregnancy.
Either side is fine; a pillow helps you get comfortable.
Don't worry about waking on your back later, just roll over.

1.q: Is dental treatment or an X-ray safe during pregnancy?
a: Routine dental care, including check-ups, cleanings and fillings, is safe and even encouraged during pregnancy, and dental X-rays are considered safe when done with proper shielding. Looking after your teeth and gums matters, because pregnancy hormones can make gums more prone to swelling and bleeding.
takeaways: Routine dental care is safe and encouraged.
Dental X-rays are safe with a lead apron and thyroid collar.
The radiation is minimal and aimed away from the abdomen.
Non-urgent work is often done in the second trimester.
Always tell your dentist you are pregnant.

1.q: Can I take hot baths, use a sauna or steam during pregnancy?
a: A warm bath is fine in pregnancy, but it is best to avoid getting too hot, and to skip saunas, steam rooms and very hot baths, especially in the first trimester. The concern is overheating, not bathing itself.
takeaways: Warm baths are fine.
Avoid saunas, steam rooms and very hot baths, especially early on.
Overheating above about 39C is the concern, linked to neural tube defects.
Keep soaks warm and short.
Get out if you feel flushed or dizzy.

1.q: What does thyroid in pregnancy mean?
a: The thyroid, a small gland in your neck, plays a big role in pregnancy, and thyroid problems, especially an underactive thyroid, are common in India. The reassuring part is that they are easily checked with a simple blood test and well managed with treatment.
takeaways: The thyroid strongly affects pregnancy, and your baby relies on yours early on.
Underactive thyroid is common in India.
It is checked with a TSH blood test early in pregnancy.
Treatment and monitoring manage it well.
Tell your doctor early if you have a thyroid condition.

1.q: What does PCOS mean for my pregnancy?
a: If you have PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome), you can absolutely have a healthy pregnancy; it simply means your pregnancy is watched a little more closely. PCOS is linked with some higher risks, which good care is designed to catch early and manage.
takeaways: PCOS is compatible with a healthy pregnancy, with closer monitoring.
It is linked with higher chances of early miscarriage, gestational diabetes and high blood pressure.
Your doctor watches blood sugar and blood pressure.
Balanced meals and activity help.
Tell your doctor early and let them guide medication.

1.q: Why do I look bloated or "showing" already in early pregnancy?
a: If you feel like you are already showing in the first weeks, it is almost always bloating rather than a baby bump. A real bump usually does not appear until the second trimester.
takeaways: Early "showing" is usually bloating, not a bump.
The real bump typically appears in the second trimester.
First-time mothers often show later, second-time or twins earlier.
Body type makes a natural difference.
Smaller meals, hydration and loose clothing help.

1.q: How does a pregnancy actually begin?
a: A pregnancy begins when a sperm meets and fertilises an egg, usually in the fallopian tube, around the time of ovulation. That single fertilised cell then starts dividing as it travels toward the womb.
takeaways: Pregnancy begins when sperm fertilises an egg, usually in the fallopian tube.
The fertilised cell divides as it travels to the womb.
Both baby and placenta grow from it.
You are dated about 2 weeks pregnant by the time it happens.
Folic acid started early matters.

1.q: What is implantation?
a: Implantation is when the tiny ball of cells from the fertilised egg settles into the lining of your womb, usually about seven to ten days after conception. This is the quiet moment a pregnancy truly takes root.
takeaways: Implantation is when the embryo settles into the womb lining, about 7 to 10 days after conception.
It lets the pregnancy draw nourishment and start making hCG.
The anchoring cells become the placenta.
Light spotting or nothing at all are both normal.
Test from your missed period.

1.q: What is the placenta and what does it do?
a: The placenta is a remarkable temporary organ that forms in pregnancy to nourish and protect your baby. It acts as your baby's lifeline, doing the work of the lungs, kidneys and digestive system until birth.
takeaways: The placenta is a temporary organ that nourishes and protects your baby.
It does the work of the lungs, kidneys and digestion.
It passes oxygen and nutrients in, and waste out.
It also makes pregnancy hormones.
Scans check its position and health.

1.q: What is the umbilical cord?
a: The umbilical cord is the flexible, rope-like link between your baby and the placenta. It is your baby's supply line, carrying oxygen and nutrients in, and waste away.
takeaways: The cord connects your baby to the placenta.
It usually has two arteries and one vein, cushioned by protective jelly.
It carries oxygen and nutrients in, and waste out.
It grows with your baby.
It is painlessly cut after birth to form the navel.

1.q: What is amniotic fluid?
a: Amniotic fluid is the clear liquid that surrounds and cushions your baby inside a protective sac, often called the "waters." It lets your baby float, move and grow safely.
takeaways: Amniotic fluid cushions and protects your baby in a sac.
It keeps a steady temperature and lets your baby move.
It helps the lungs and gut practise and mature.
The amount is balanced by your body and checked on scans.
Hydration supports healthy levels.

1.q: Are bleeding gums normal in pregnancy?
a: Sore or bleeding gums are common in pregnancy and usually nothing to worry about. Pregnancy hormones make the gums more sensitive and prone to swelling and bleeding, sometimes called pregnancy gingivitis.
takeaways: Sore, bleeding gums are common and usually harmless.
Caused by hormones making gums more sensitive.
Keep brushing gently and floss.
Warm salt-water rinses soothe.
Routine dental care is safe and worthwhile.

1.q: Is a stuffy or bleeding nose normal in pregnancy?
a: A stuffy, runny or occasionally bleeding nose is common in pregnancy and usually harmless. It is caused by rising hormones and increased blood flow to the lining of your nose, sometimes called pregnancy rhinitis.
takeaways: A stuffy or lightly bleeding nose is common and harmless.
Caused by hormones and increased blood flow (pregnancy rhinitis).
Hydration, saline drops and a humidifier help.
Pinch and lean forward for a nosebleed.
Check with your doctor before any medicine.

1.q: What can I do for a cold, cough or fever in pregnancy?
a: A common cold or cough in pregnancy is usually uncomfortable rather than dangerous, and it tends to pass in about a week with rest and fluids. A fever, though, is worth taking seriously, especially in early pregnancy.
takeaways: Colds and coughs are usually harmless and pass with rest and fluids.
Steam, gargles and honey soothe symptoms.
A fever, especially early on, should be checked.
Do not take any medicine without your doctor's guidance.
Watch for breathing trouble or dehydration.

1.q: Can I keep working and lifting during pregnancy?
a: Most women can safely keep working through pregnancy, including into the later months. The main things to be sensible about are heavy lifting, long periods of standing, and overexertion.
takeaways: Most women can safely keep working through pregnancy.
Avoid heavy lifting and long standing, and don't overexert.
Lift with your knees and ask for help.
Take breaks, hydrate and rest.
Discuss a physically demanding job with your doctor.

1.q: Which vaccines do I need in pregnancy?
a: Some vaccines are recommended in every pregnancy to protect you and your baby, mainly tetanus-containing vaccines and the flu (influenza) vaccine. A few others, the live vaccines, are avoided during pregnancy.
takeaways: Tetanus-containing vaccines and the inactivated flu vaccine are recommended in every pregnancy.
In India, tetanus (TT/Td/Tdap) is routine antenatal care.
Tdap also protects the newborn from whooping cough.
Inactivated vaccines cannot cause illness.
Live vaccines like MMR and chickenpox are avoided in pregnancy.

2.q: What happens in the second month of pregnancy?
a: The second month covers weeks 5 to 8, and it is one of the busiest stretches of your whole pregnancy. Your baby's major organs begin forming, and this is often when early symptoms like nausea and tiredness become more noticeable.
takeaways: Month 2 is weeks 5 to 8, the embryonic period.
Your baby's major organs begin forming now.
Nausea, fatigue and tender breasts often intensify.
Keep up folic acid, small meals, rest and fluids.
The first scan and booking bloods usually happen this month.

2.q: How is my baby developing in the second month?
a: The second month, weeks 5 to 8, is when your baby changes from a tiny cluster of cells into a recognisable embryo with the beginnings of a heart, brain, limbs and major organs. By the end of it, your baby is around the size of a black bean.
takeaways: Month 2 is the embryonic period, weeks 5 to 8.
The heart starts beating and is often seen on a scan by week 6.
Limb buds, facial features and major organs form.
By week 8 your baby is about the size of a black bean.
After week 8 to 10, the embryo is called a fetus.

2.q: My morning sickness is at its worst now. What helps?
a: Morning sickness often peaks around weeks 8 to 10, so feeling at your worst in the second month is completely normal. It is usually harmless, and for most women it starts easing by the end of the first trimester, around weeks 12 to 14.
takeaways: Nausea often peaks around weeks 8 to 10.
It is usually harmless and eases by weeks 12 to 14.
Small frequent meals and eating before rising help.
Ginger and small sips of fluid are reliable comforts.
Avoid triggers, rest, and never self-medicate.

2.q: When is morning sickness more than normal (hyperemesis gravidarum)?
a: Most pregnancy nausea is ordinary morning sickness, but a small number of women develop a more severe form called hyperemesis gravidarum, where the vomiting is so frequent that you cannot keep food or fluids down. It is far less common, and it is very treatable with the right care.
takeaways: Hyperemesis gravidarum is severe, persistent vomiting, unlike ordinary nausea.
Signs: can't keep fluids down, little or dark urine, dizziness, weight loss.
It can lead to dehydration and needs medical care.
More likely with twins, a first pregnancy, or a past history.
Treatment, sometimes fluids by drip, helps you both.

2.q: What are the signs of a miscarriage, and what should I do?
a: A miscarriage is the loss of a pregnancy in the first 20 weeks, most often in the early weeks. The most common signs are vaginal bleeding and cramping, though it is important to know that light bleeding is common in early pregnancy and does not usually mean a miscarriage.
takeaways: Miscarriage is pregnancy loss before 20 weeks, most often early.
Common signs are bleeding and cramping, but light bleeding is often harmless.
Most early losses are due to chromosomal chance, not anything you did.
Contact your doctor for any bleeding; use pads, not tampons.
Many who bleed early still have a healthy pregnancy.

2.q: I'm pregnant after a miscarriage. How do I cope with the worry?
a: Feeling anxious, guarded, or unable to fully celebrate when you are pregnant again after a loss is completely normal. Many women feel this way, and it does not mean anything is wrong with you or the pregnancy.
takeaways: Anxiety after a loss is normal and very common.
One miscarriage usually does not raise the risk of another.
Most women go on to have a healthy pregnancy.
Take it one milestone at a time, and lean on support.
Seek a counsellor if worry feels heavy or constant.

2.q: Can I eat papaya, pineapple and other "heat" foods in pregnancy?
a: Ripe papaya and pineapple are both safe to enjoy in moderation during pregnancy. The one to avoid is raw or unripe (green) papaya. The wider belief that these are dangerous "heat" foods is largely a myth.
takeaways: Ripe papaya and pineapple are safe in moderation.
Avoid raw or unripe (green) papaya.
The bromelain and "heat food" fears are largely myths.
FOGSI and ACOG do not single these fruits out.
Check with your doctor if your pregnancy is high-risk.

2.q: Is ghee good during pregnancy, and how much?
a: Ghee is safe and nourishing during pregnancy in moderation, as part of a balanced diet. What is not true is the popular belief that eating extra ghee, especially late in pregnancy, eases labour or ensures a normal delivery.
takeaways: Ghee is safe and nourishing in moderation.
It provides healthy fats and fat-soluble vitamins.
The "ghee eases labour" belief has no evidence.
Delivery is decided by medical factors, not diet.
Watch portions with gestational diabetes or fast weight gain.

2.q: How much weight should I gain in pregnancy?
a: How much weight to gain depends on your weight before pregnancy. As a general guide, a woman starting at a healthy weight gains around 11 to 16 kilograms over the whole pregnancy, with only about 1 to 2 kilograms in the first trimester.
takeaways: Recommended gain depends on your pre-pregnancy BMI.
Healthy-range women gain about 11 to 16 kg total.
Only about 1 to 2 kg comes in the first trimester.
India uses Asian BMI cut-offs; steady gain matters most.
Don't diet to limit gain, and don't eat for two.

2.q: Which exercises and yoga are safe in early pregnancy, and what should I avoid?
a: In a healthy pregnancy, gentle exercise and prenatal yoga are not only safe but encouraged, aiming for about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week. The key is to choose low-impact movement and avoid a short list of risky poses and activities.
takeaways: Aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week.
Safe: walking, swimming, prenatal yoga, pelvic floor work.
Avoid falls, overheating and hot yoga.
Skip inversions, deep twists, backbends and forceful breath-holding.
Start gently and check with your doctor if high-risk.

2.q: Are heartburn and acidity normal in pregnancy?
a: Heartburn and acidity, a burning feeling in the chest or throat, often after eating, are very common in pregnancy and usually harmless. They tend to start in the early months and can increase later on.
takeaways: Heartburn and acidity are common and usually harmless.
Caused by hormones relaxing a valve, and later the womb pressing up.
Small frequent meals and avoiding triggers help.
Don't lie down right after eating; raise your head at night.
Check with your doctor before taking anything for it.

2.q: Why do I have so much saliva in early pregnancy?
a: Producing more saliva than usual, sometimes enough that you want to spit it out, is a harmless and fairly common early pregnancy symptom. It is called ptyalism, and it usually settles as the first trimester ends.
takeaways: Extra saliva (ptyalism) is harmless and common early on.
It is linked to hormones and nausea.
It usually eases by the second trimester.
Sip water, chew gum, and keep up oral care.

2.q: Why is my skin getting darker in patches during pregnancy?
a: Darker patches on the face and a dark line down the middle of the belly are common, normal skin changes in pregnancy. They are caused by hormones increasing the pigment in your skin, and they usually fade after birth.
takeaways: Facial patches (melasma) and a belly line (linea nigra) are normal.
Caused by hormones raising skin pigment.
More noticeable on deeper skin tones; sun darkens facial patches.
Usually fade within months after birth.
Use sun protection; avoid strong lightening creams.

2.q: My pregnancy symptoms come and go, or have faded. Is that normal?
a: It is completely normal for early pregnancy symptoms to come and go, feel stronger some days and barely there on others, or ease off as you near the end of the first trimester. Symptoms fluctuating does not mean anything is wrong.
takeaways: Early symptoms naturally come and go.
Hormone levels rise and dip day to day.
Many symptoms ease around weeks 11 to 14 as the placenta takes over.
Few symptoms can be perfectly normal too.
Check only if all symptoms vanish suddenly with bleeding or cramping.

2.q: Can I eat fish and seafood during pregnancy?
a: In most pregnancies you can eat fish, and it is good for you and your baby, as long as you choose low-mercury fish, cook it well, and keep to about two servings a week. Only a few large fish, and all raw or undercooked seafood, are best avoided.
takeaways: Fish is nourishing; aim for about two servings a week.
Choose low-mercury fish and cook them well.
Good Indian options: pomfret, rawas, bangda, sardines, rohu, catla, cooked prawns.
Avoid shark, swordfish, king mackerel and tilefish.
Avoid all raw or undercooked seafood.

2.q: Does saffron (kesar) milk make the baby fairer?
a: A warm cup of kesar (saffron) milk is a cherished part of many Indian pregnancies, and small culinary amounts are generally considered safe. The popular belief that it makes the baby fairer, though, is a myth.
takeaways: Small culinary amounts of saffron are generally safe.
It does not make the baby fairer; complexion is genetic.
Avoid large or medicinal doses.
Use a few strands of pure saffron.
Check with your doctor in the first trimester or if high-risk.

2.q: Is it safe to travel during pregnancy?
a: In a healthy pregnancy, travel is generally safe, and the second trimester is usually the most comfortable time. Early pregnancy travel is fine too, though nausea and tiredness can make it less pleasant, so shorter trips are easier for now. Do check with your doctor before long, international or high-altitude travel, or if your pregnancy is high-risk.
takeaways: Travel is generally safe; the second trimester is most comfortable.
Move your legs and hydrate on trips over a few hours.
Wear the seatbelt low, under your bump.
Flying is usually fine before about 36 weeks.
Check with your doctor for long, international or high-risk travel.

2.q: What warning signs mean I should call my doctor?
a: Most pregnancy symptoms are uncomfortable but harmless. A few, though, are worth acting on: call your doctor promptly for heavy bleeding, severe tummy pain, a severe headache with blurred vision or sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, persistent vomiting, fainting, or one-sided leg pain or breathlessness. This is about awareness, not fear; most pregnancies never involve any of them.
takeaways: Most symptoms are normal; only a few need prompt action.
Call for heavy bleeding, severe pain, or a severe headache with vision changes or swelling.
Call for fever, persistent vomiting, fainting, leg pain or breathlessness.
Later, reduced baby movements or leaking fluid warrant a call.
Trust your instinct; if something feels wrong, check.

2.q: What is a molar pregnancy?
a: A molar pregnancy is a rare condition where the tissue that would normally become the placenta grows abnormally, so the pregnancy cannot develop as usual. It is uncommon, and although it means this pregnancy will not continue, it is very treatable.
takeaways: A molar pregnancy is a rare, abnormal growth of placental tissue.
It happens by chance, not because of anything you did.
Signs include unusual bleeding, severe nausea, high hCG, fast womb growth.
It is found on a scan and treated by removing the tissue.
Follow-up hCG checks are needed; most women later have a healthy pregnancy.

2.q: What is a vanishing twin?
a: A vanishing twin is when an early scan shows twins, but one twin stops developing and is gently reabsorbed by the body, usually in the first trimester. In most cases the remaining twin continues to grow and develop normally.
takeaways: A vanishing twin is when one early twin stops developing and is reabsorbed.
It usually happens in the first trimester.
The remaining twin usually continues normally.
There may be light spotting or no symptoms.
Mixed emotions are natural; support is available.

2.q: Is it safe to eat street food and outside food in pregnancy?
a: Street food like pani puri, chaat and cut fruit is best kept to a minimum in pregnancy, because the main risk is a stomach infection from unhygienic handling or water, not the food itself. If you do have it, choose freshly cooked, piping-hot items, skip anything raw or watery, and contact your doctor if you get a bad stomach with fever or severe cramps.
takeaways: The risk is infection from hygiene and water, not the dish itself.
Lowered immunity makes food poisoning more likely.
If you indulge, eat it freshly cooked and piping hot.
Skip raw chutneys, cut fruit, ice and unfiltered water.
Home versions with filtered water are safest.

2.q: Can I eat curd, and does it cause a cold for the baby?
a: Curd (dahi) is safe and good for you in pregnancy, as long as it is made from pasteurised or properly boiled milk. The common belief that curd or cold foods give the baby a cold is a myth.
takeaways: Curd is safe and nourishing in pregnancy.
Use pasteurised or boiled-milk curd; avoid raw or street-set.
"Curd causes a cold" is a myth; colds are viral.
It gives calcium, protein and probiotics.
Room-temperature curd is fine if cold feels uncomfortable.

2.q: Is coconut water good during pregnancy?
a: Coconut water (nariyal pani) is a safe, hydrating and refreshing choice in pregnancy, enjoyed in normal amounts. It will not, however, make your baby fairer or give thicker hair, those are myths.
takeaways: Coconut water is safe and hydrating in normal amounts.
Rich in electrolytes; good in the heat.
It does not make the baby fair or change hair; that is genetic.
It does not replace a balanced diet or supplements.
Check with your doctor if you have gestational diabetes.

2.q: Which supplements do I need in pregnancy besides folic acid?
a: Besides folic acid, most pregnancies need iron and calcium, and often vitamin D, with others like vitamin B12, iodine and omega-3 depending on your diet and health. Your doctor decides exactly what you need, so take supplements on their advice rather than choosing your own.
takeaways: Beyond folic acid, iron and calcium are usually needed, often vitamin D.
B12, iodine and omega-3 matter more on plant-based diets.
Your doctor decides what and how much.
Space iron and calcium apart; iron likes vitamin C, not tea.
Don't self-add high-dose supplements.

2.q: Why can't I sleep well in early pregnancy?
a: Trouble sleeping is common in early pregnancy and, while tiring, is not harmful to your baby. It is usually down to hormones, nausea and extra trips to the bathroom, and it often eases in the second trimester.
takeaways: Sleep trouble is common early on and not harmful to the baby.
Caused by hormones, nausea, urination and a busy mind.
A calming routine and less evening screen time help.
Side-sleep with a pillow; nap when you can.
Never take a sleep aid without your doctor.

2.q: Is it normal to feel breathless or have a racing heart in early pregnancy?
a: Feeling a little breathless or noticing your heart beating faster or harder is common in pregnancy and usually normal, even early on. It comes from the natural changes in your breathing and circulation, though a few signs, noted below, are worth checking.
takeaways: Mild breathlessness and palpitations are common and usually normal.
Caused by deeper breathing and more blood being pumped.
Anaemia can worsen breathlessness.
Rest, hydrate and keep iron levels up.
